name: Benzphetamine

lead: Benzphetamine (Didrex) is an older prescription appetite suppressant related to amphetamine. It reduces hunger so people eat less and lose weight, working toward a leaner look.

It is thought to increase norepinephrine and dopamine release in the brain's feeding centers, and the body converts it to amphetamine and methamphetamine. In the US it is labelled as a short-term add-on, lasting a few weeks, to a reduced-calorie diet for people with a BMI of 30 or higher.

paras: It is taken as a pill under prescription for a short period alongside a calorie-restricted diet. The label states it is not for long-term use.

Reported effects include raised heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia and restlessness. The label cites an association between long-term anorectic use and pulmonary hypertension and contraindicates use in pregnancy. It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US.

angle.text: Benzphetamine is a stimulant appetite suppressant that lowers calorie intake and leads to weight loss and a leaner look. It is a prescription obesity medication labelled for a few weeks of use.

lead: Benzphetamine (brand name Didrex, also spelled benzfetamine) is a prescription appetite suppressant. It is used to reduce hunger so that a person eating fewer calories can lose body fat, which in turn changes how the face and body look: a smaller waist, a slimmer face and more visible muscle definition. In the United States it is labelled as a short-term adjunct, a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted weight-reduction regimen for adults with a body mass index of 30 or higher who have not responded to diet and exercise alone.[1][2]

It belongs to the sympathomimetic amine class alongside phentermine, diethylpropion and phendimetrazine, the older anorectics approved only for short-term use.[3][4] It is described as a prodrug that the body converts into amphetamine and methamphetamine, and it is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US, which Wikipedia notes is unusual for an amphetamine-related drug.[2][2]

Benzphetamine is a medical drug, not a cosmetic product, and the label does not describe it for cosmetic weight reduction.[1][2] Within appearance and bodybuilding culture it appears mostly as one of the older fat-loss prescription stimulants, and it is also named on anti-doping prohibited-stimulant lists that circulate in training forums.[5]
infobox: Schedule III controlled substance, prescription only

paras: The US label indicates benzphetamine for the management of exogenous obesity as a short-term adjunct to caloric restriction in patients with a BMI of 30 kg/m2 or higher who have not responded to appropriate weight-reduction efforts.[1] Reviews group it with diethylpropion, phendimetrazine and phentermine as the sympathomimetic drugs approved only for short-term use, in contrast with newer medications approved for longer treatment.[3][4]

Grokipedia reports that the drug was approved in 1960 and that trials showed modest additional weight loss over placebo that plateaued after the early weeks as tolerance developed; that source is AI-generated and these figures were not checked against trial reports.[6]

Appetite suppressants are discussed as adjuncts to diet and physical activity, and a drug-insight review describes them as helpful adjuncts for selected patients aiming to achieve and maintain weight loss.[4] Any change in appearance from benzphetamine comes through that fat loss. The US label states the drug is intended for obesity management rather than cosmetic use.[1]

The label lists palpitations, tachycardia and elevated blood pressure among cardiovascular effects, along with central nervous system effects such as overstimulation, restlessness and insomnia.[1] It warns against combining benzphetamine with other anorectic agents, including over-the-counter and herbal products.[1]

The label cites a case-control study in which anorectic drugs used for longer than three months were associated with a 23-fold increase in the risk of pulmonary hypertension, a rare and often fatal condition.[1] Valvular heart disease has been reported with some other anorectics such as fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine; the label states that no such cases had been reported with benzphetamine.[1] The drug is contraindicated in pregnancy.[1] Contraindications also include advanced arteriosclerosis, symptomatic cardiovascular disease, hyperthyroidism, glaucoma, agitation, a history of drug misuse and recent monoamine oxidase inhibitor use.[2]

A review of obesity-drug safety notes that the safety record of obesity drugs has historically been poor, citing withdrawn drugs, and reviews the safety of benzphetamine among the currently available agents.[7] Wikipedia lists dependence liability as high.[2]

Benzphetamine is thought to act like other amphetamines by promoting release of norepinephrine and dopamine in the hypothalamic feeding centre, reducing appetite; its exact mechanism is not fully established.[2] Tolerance and tachyphylaxis to the appetite-suppressing effect are described for the class.[2]

Wikipedia gives an elimination half-life of about 4 to 6 hours and notes that the drug is highly protein-bound and converted in the body to dextroamphetamine and dextromethamphetamine.[2] Grokipedia gives a longer half-life, so published figures differ.[6] A 1987 human laboratory study examined the reinforcing and subjective effects of several anorectics, benzphetamine among them, in healthy volunteers.[8]

Grokipedia gives a US approval year of 1960.[6] Legal status varies: Schedule III in the US, Schedule I in Canada, Class C in the UK, prescription-only (Schedule 4) in Australia, Class F2 in Brazil, and restricted to authorised scientific use in Germany.[2] It is the parent compound of the related anorectic clobenzorex.[2]

Benzphetamine appears on World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited stimulant lists that T Nation members have posted in supplement and drug-testing threads, and a 2003 thread lists Didrex among several prescription drugs a poster described holding.[5][9]

Published human work includes a 1969 controlled trial comparing single and divided doses of benzphetamine hydrochloride for pharmacodynamic activity, and a 1987 controlled trial of its reinforcing and subjective effects in healthy volunteers.[8][10] Reviews of weight-loss pharmacotherapy summarise it as one of the short-term sympathomimetic options.[3][4] A 2025 Cureus editorial discusses a theoretical potential of benzphetamine in ADHD.[11] No studies found examining benzphetamine for facial appearance or cosmetic outcomes.

lore.intro: Benzphetamine is rarely the subject of looksmaxxing threads; in bodybuilding forums it turns up in lists of banned stimulants and in poster inventories of prescription drugs.[5][9]
